$comment: The ledger. Every mistake made or found in this build names a GUARD that prevents its return, and tools/check_lessons.py fails the build if a lesson has no guard, if a named guard does not exist, or if a test suite is not registered to run. A lesson written down but not enforced is a promise; a lesson with a guard is a fact about the code.

lessons.mistake: A fixture factory stranded a distractor with no rationale whenever the key moved position — the answer-position de-bias defect, reproduced inside the test fixtures themselves.
lessons.caughtBy: the clean fixture failed its own distractor-coverage proof

lessons.mistake: A proof blanked the KEY's explanation instead of a distractor's, so it asserted a defect the gate correctly ignores.
lessons.caughtBy: the gate stayed green and the test went red

lessons.mistake: The truncation gate stripped trailing DIGITS, turning a complete stem ending '...the Homestead Act of 1862?' into '...Act of' and flagging a dangling preposition.
lessons.caughtBy: reading the 484 findings instead of trusting the count

guards.contains: a complete stem ending in a year + '?' is NOT truncation

lessons.mistake: The truncation gate flagged TCAP-style completion stems that legitimately end on a colon or dash.
lessons.caughtBy: reading the findings

guards.contains: a TCAP completion stem ending in a colon is NOT truncation

lessons.mistake: Answer-position de-bias failed on a 27/25/24/24 split — statistically significant at n=3,844, practically unexploitable. An alarm that fires on the harmless trains people to ignore it.
lessons.caughtBy: the gate went red on a bank that was fine

guards.contains: a 27/25/24/24 split at large n PASSES

lessons.mistake: Migration was routed on difflib character similarity, which is ANTI-correlated with alignment: 0.79 was a pure bullet reorder, 0.89 had deleted the Clayton Antitrust Act, 0.94 had changed its verb.
lessons.caughtBy: reading real standard pairs before choosing a threshold

lessons.mistake: Element matching read the item's DISTRACTORS, so a question about the 17th Amendment was quarantined because a wrong choice mentioned the 18th.
lessons.caughtBy: sampling quarantined items and reading them

guards.contains: item testing the 17th Amendment does not match dropped '18th Amendment'

lessons.mistake: 'United States v. Nixon' vs 'United States vs. Nixon' read as a deletion — 49 items wrongly quarantined by punctuation.
lessons.caughtBy: sampling quarantined items

guards.contains: v. / vs. punctuation not read as a deletion

lessons.mistake: Rewording read as deletion: Tennessee's role appeared 'dropped' when only the nickname 'Perfect 36' had gone, and 'suffragettes'->'suffragists' read as a removal.
lessons.caughtBy: checking the highest-stakes quarantine by hand

lessons.mistake: Signals were too generic to identify anything: '18th Amendment' reduced to 'Amendment', and 'American' matched almost every item in a US History bank.
lessons.caughtBy: a pinned test going red

guards.contains: 'Amendment' alone is not a usable signal

lessons.mistake: teacher-side-isolation reported PASS over 3,986 items while judging ZERO of them. The empty-scan guard watched the outer scan; the gate's own filter removed everything.
lessons.caughtBy: checking what the gate actually inspected, not what it scanned

guards.contains: no student surfaces present -> NOT MEASURED, not PASS

lessons.mistake: distractor-coverage carried the same latent vacuity: it would have passed a bank containing no selected-response items at all.
lessons.caughtBy: auditing every gate for the L11 pattern

guards.contains: distractor-coverage over a bank with no selected-response is NOT MEASURED

lessons.mistake: A PDF scan returned zero hits for 'reporting category' — and zero for 'Compromise of 1877', which is certainly in that document. A broken extractor's zero is indistinguishable from a real zero and reads like an answer.
lessons.caughtBy: sanity-checking the extractor against a string known to be present

guards.contains: a broken extraction REFUSES to report an absence

lessons.mistake: A reporting-category PLAUSIBILITY gate was designed that PASSED the very defect it existed to catch — a Bessemer-process item filed under Government and Civics, whose standard carries strands C and P.
lessons.caughtBy: measuring the proposed gate against the known-bad item before shipping it

lessons.mistake: A pass tally was reported to the owner that INCLUDED a vacuous pass ('4/11'), because the runner counted a NOT-MEASURED gate as passing.
lessons.caughtBy: the L11 investigation

guards.contains: NOT MEASURED is not a pass
the runner does not count NOT MEASURED as a pass

lessons.mistake: A gate green against an empty set reads exactly like a clean pass.
lessons.caughtBy: stated by the owner up front; built in from the start

lessons.mistake: Sixteen gates were built and every one measured how the bank was MADE; none measured what it is ABOUT. They all passed a bank in which 1,680 items (42%) contain no named element of the standard they are filed under — a Vietnam anti-war question under 'the founding of the United Nations', a Korea question under 'prosperity and consumerism in the 1950s'. This is the exact failure the owner described in the opening brief.
lessons.caughtBy: probing the bank for defects no existing gate was looking for

guards.contains: an item CLAIMING 'evidenced' with no evidence FAILS

lessons.mistake: Answer-position de-bias was gated, but no gate measured any other test-taking cue. The key is the LONGEST choice in 53.3% of items against 25% by chance — a student can beat the bank without reading a single stem, which is the same defect as '60% of keys are C' and was equally invisible.
lessons.caughtBy: asking what other cues a structural gate cannot see

guards.contains: a bank where the key is ALWAYS longest FAILS

lessons.mistake: Nothing checked for duplicate items. 44 items across 21 groups share a stem with another item under a different id, so one question can appear twice on a form and be counted twice toward coverage.
lessons.caughtBy: probing the migrated bank

guards.contains: two ids sharing one stem FAILS

lessons.mistake: A matcher tuned for DETECTION was reused for ASSIGNMENT. The relevance gate may be loose — a loose gate simply flags fewer items, which is conservative. The re-home scorer inherited that looseness and accepted any single generic word, proposing to move a Gilded Age Carnegie item to a standard about the space race because both contain 'industry', and a 'Gilded Age' item to another because it contains 'recall'. A wrong move creates a confident mislabel, which is worse than the flag it replaces.
lessons.caughtBy: sampling eight proposals before applying any of them

guards.contains: a bare generic word is never evidence

lessons.mistake: The standard-relevance gate matched only the CHECKLIST — the words after 'including' — so items correctly filed under US.74 were flagged as off-standard because 'Brown v. Board of Education' appears in that standard's stem, not after an 'including'. The gate over-flagged and the triage tool then proposed moving correctly-filed items.
lessons.caughtBy: three of eight sampled proposals being Brown v. Board items

guards.contains: a correctly-filed Brown v. Board item is NOT flagged

lessons.mistake: tools/rehome.py re-implemented the relevance test instead of asking the gate, and the two disagreed by 437 items — the same defect as a status report that recomputes its own gate results.
lessons.caughtBy: the triage tool reporting 2,100 flagged while the gate reported 1,663

lessons.mistake: Re-home evidence was taken from the key explanation as well as the stem, so a passing mention decided a move: an Eisenhower 'Modern Republicanism' item went to the New Deal and a United Nations item to Pearl Harbor. The stem is what an item ASKS; the explanation may corroborate but must not decide.
lessons.caughtBy: sampling ten proposals and finding four wrong for the same reason

guards.contains: The deciding evidence must be in the STEM
a name appearing only in the EXPLANATION cannot move an item

lessons.mistake: Content quality and ALIGNMENT CONFIDENCE were collapsed into one axis, so an unverified label read as a verdict on the question. 1,320 items with fully intact stems, choices, explanations and bilingual fields were described to the owner as items that could not be saved, when nothing had been deleted and every one was still usable. The owner caught it: 'The content is the same? It's just the alignment as my concern.' alignmentStatus is now its own field, and the gate fails a DISHONEST CLAIM rather than the existence of an unverified item.
lessons.caughtBy: the owner, reading a status report that confused a label with a loss

guards.contains: its CONTENT is untouched by the label

lessons.mistake: A bulk edit had replaced PUBLICATION TITLES with REPOSITORY names across the primary-source items, leaving the date intact and a dangling noun behind: Langston Hughes's 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' read 'first published in Library of Congress, NAACP Records (loc.gov), June 1921' when it was published in The Crisis. A repository is where a scan lives, not where a work was published. No gate looked at citations at all, and these are the DBQ and constructed-response items an adoption reviewer reads first.
lessons.caughtBy: reading six real items before authoring, rather than starting to write

guards.contains: naming a repository as where a scan is AVAILABLE is not a defect

lessons.mistake: The citation CORRECTION SHEET matched its proposals against the whole item, so a Marcus Garvey speech was proposed the publication of a Langston Hughes poem — the Garvey excerpt contains the words 'I, too' in its prose. A tool built to fix wrong attributions produced a wrong attribution, which is the L20 lesson again: an ASSIGNMENT must match on the narrowest evidence, here the citation line alone.
lessons.caughtBy: reading the generated correction sheet instead of trusting it

lessons.mistake: No gate looked at whether the SPANISH was Spanish. 1,144 items carry a textEs that is a verbatim copy of the English, and 408 carry a word-substitution pseudo-translation — 'The programs violated the 5th enmienda's protection against government taking of property', 'Congreso had rarely had the authority to levy taxes'. The second is worse than nothing because it LOOKS translated. 93 of them claimed translationStatus 'complete', which is a false accessibility claim on a district-facing product.
lessons.caughtBy: reading a truncation finding and noticing the Spanish choice set differed from the English

guards.contains: a bilingual claim is an accessibility claim
an acronym identical in both languages is not a defect

lessons.mistake: The item spec says the key's explanation is 'why it is right, not a restatement of it', and nothing measured that. 920 items either open by repeating the key verbatim or carry an explanation IDENTICAL to their own dokRationale — one terse editorial note ('DOK 1: identify core dynamic of sharecropping') standing in for two different jobs.
lessons.caughtBy: reading six real items before authoring them

guards.contains: an explanation identical to the dokRationale FAILS

lessons.mistake: blueprint-conformance measured a 3,986-item BANK against a 564-item target and reported 681 findings, none of them actionable. Exact-count conformance failing in either direction is right for a FORM — 7 items where the blueprint says 6 is a defective form — but for a bank 'too many items' is depth, not drift. The gate was reporting a units error as a defect.
lessons.caughtBy: asking what a failing gate was actually asking anyone to DO

guards.contains: is depth, and depth is what lets forms

lessons.mistake: Nine items carried their ENTIRE body inside the stem — question, then all four options inline, with an answer-key marker surviving the paste ('…? H It committed the United States to supporting free peoples… B. It authorized…'). Rendered on a form the student reads every option twice and sees the marker. Found only because a form gate fired on a rendered PDF; no bank gate looked at student-visible text for key material.
lessons.caughtBy: form-key-leakage firing on page 4 of a rendered student PDF

guards.contains: a stem containing its own choice list FAILS

lessons.mistake: The form builder never built to the blueprint. select() took the first N items per standard by id and never looked at DOK or item type, so a form drawn from a deep standard came out six multiple-choice items at the wrong levels. A form blueprint is a set of SLOTS and selection has to fill them — the gate existed before the builder could satisfy it.
lessons.caughtBy: wiring form-blueprint into the runner and watching it fail on a form I had built

guards.contains: A form blueprint is a set of SLOTS
form: one item OVER the tier FAILS

lessons.mistake: The form builder left key placement to a hash, so FORM-A rendered 42% of its keys on position D. The de-bias gate had existed for several commits and could not pass, because nothing in the BUILDER was trying to satisfy it. A gate the builder cannot satisfy is a gate that stays red and gets ignored.
lessons.caughtBy: running the scoped form check and seeing a gate that had never been green

lessons.mistake: Fixing the longest-choice cue over-corrected FORM-A from 66.7% to 0.0%, and the gate PASSED it. 'The longest option is never right' is exactly as learnable as the reverse, and the gate was one-sided. A remediation that trips the opposite version of the same defect is not a fix.
lessons.caughtBy: the suspiciously perfect 0.0% reading

lessons.mistake: The scoped form runner ran the BANK-level key-position gate over a form. That gate reads each item's stored correctAnswer id, so it reported D at 42% while the form actually rendered 3/3/3/3 — a distribution no student would ever see. A gate must measure the artifact at the level the artifact exists.
lessons.caughtBy: the rendered surface disagreeing with the gate that was judging it

lessons.mistake: Introducing N/A — a gate with an honest reason for having nothing to judge — risked re-opening L11, where a gate judging nothing reported PASS. The exception is real (citation-integrity on a form whose items carry no citations) but it is the kind of exception that swallows the rule. So the reason is REQUIRED, N/A is never reported or counted as PASS, and a gate cannot claim N/A while its population exists.
lessons.caughtBy: noticing the exception was the shape of the defect it sat next to

guards.contains: The loophole this could open is obvious
citation-integrity does NOT claim N/A when a citation is present

lessons.mistake: The relevance gate used alignment.signals(), which falls back to bare content words when an element has no proper noun. 'Support for conservation' yielded 'Support', and a constructed response about the 19th Amendment and W.E.B. Du Bois claimed Theodore Roosevelt's standard on that one word. This is L10 reappearing in a SECOND matcher — fixing a rule in one place is not fixing the rule.
lessons.caughtBy: attempting a second form and reading what its slots had been filled with

lessons.mistake: An item is 'aligned' if it matches ANY of its standard codes, but a form prints it under ONE. A constructed response carrying US.17, US.18 and US.19 would have printed under a Theodore Roosevelt heading while being about women's suffrage. A form heading is a claim, and nothing was checking it.
lessons.caughtBy: the same second-form attempt

guards.contains: an item printed under a standard it does not name FAILS

lessons.mistake: Relevance was judged on the key explanation as well as the stem and choices — and explanations are AUTHORED, including by this system. A rationale written here for a Hoover-era RFC item mentioned 'the New Deal's direct relief' in passing, and that alone made the item look aligned to the New Deal standard it was mis-filed under. Content written to EXPLAIN an item must never be what proves the item belongs somewhere.
lessons.caughtBy: the new form-standard-relevance gate failing a form already declared green

guards.contains: must never prove where it belongs
the key explanation is excluded from the relevance haystack

lessons.mistake: Standards write '19th Amendment'; items commonly write 'Nineteenth Amendment'. Literal substring matching read 92 occurrences of word-spelled ordinals in student-visible text as naming nothing, so correctly filed amendment questions would have been flagged off-standard.
lessons.caughtBy: a regression test failing on a fixture that was itself correct

guards.contains: a WORD-spelled ordinal matches a numeral-written standard

lessons.mistake: form_readiness.py computed which standards could build a form using its own placement rule while forms.py used another, so readiness reported 35 buildable standards when the builder could reach 17. L22 for the third time: two implementations of one rule always diverge.
lessons.caughtBy: readiness and the builder disagreeing after the placement rule tightened

guards.contains: Same placement rule the FORM BUILDER uses

lessons.mistake: Human approval of authored content arrived as a sentence in conversation. Left there it is something the build 'knows' — which is how an unreviewed item ends up looking reviewed, and how an approval's SCOPE quietly widens. The authored rationales carry historical claims no gate can check ('Spain had lost its mainland American colonies eighty years earlier'), so the review CLAIM is the thing to gate, exactly as with alignment and translation.
lessons.caughtBy: recording an approval and asking what would stop the next item from claiming it

guards.contains: an item CLAIMING review that no record names FAILS
authored content that is silently settled FAILS

lessons.mistake: Rewriting tools/gates/coverage.py by slicing from one function to the END of the file silently deleted two gates defined after it. The runner crashed on an AttributeError, which was LUCK — had those gates been referenced only in a branch that did not run, the deletion would have been invisible and the artifact would simply have stopped being checked for those defects.
lessons.caughtBy: a crash that could easily not have happened

lessons.mistake: The flat form blueprint required a document-based item for every standard — 94 against 30 in the bank — blocking 71 standards behind a shortage no authoring on existing items could fix. The deeper reason it could never be met: DOK-4 is structurally impossible in a four-option selected-response item (the bank holds 610/702/627 mcq at DOK 1/2/3 and ZERO at DOK-4, correctly), so a DOK-4 slot IS a requirement for an extended item. Tiering states that ceiling on the form instead of pretending; buildable standards went 17 -> 57. Tiering is not a loosening: within its declared tier a form must still match slot for slot.
lessons.caughtBy: measuring DOK availability by item type before choosing a new blueprint shape

guards.contains: a form claiming a tier it does not fill FAILS
a form declaring NO tier FAILS

lessons.mistake: form_readiness.py was broken by the tiered blueprint — it read a flat `form.dok` that no longer existed — and its stale CSV was committed and sent to the owner anyway, because the regeneration ran with `>/dev/null 2>&1` and nobody read the exit code. Suppressing a tool's output is how a broken tool ships. Then, fixing it, the SAME slicing mistake as L42 deleted the block that built its data.
lessons.caughtBy: the owner asking what the next step was, which meant running the tool for real

guards.contains: every committed report can be regenerated
readiness reports the tier a pool can actually reach

lessons.mistake: Relevance evidence included the DISTRACTORS. A Carter-era Panama Canal Treaties item was filed under Cold War superpower competition because a WRONG choice mentioned 'the Soviet Union'. 141 items were relevant to a standard only through a distractor. This is L07 — the rule the re-home matcher had used since the beginning — finally arriving at the relevance layer. There is now ONE definition of what an item is about, alignment.subject_text: stem plus the key, never the distractors and never the authored explanation.
lessons.caughtBy: reading the items a second form had selected, before authoring them

lessons.mistake: relevance_scan RE-IMPLEMENTED the matcher instead of calling alignment.relevant_to, and its copy forgot to lowercase the haystack — so a proper-noun signal could never match. L22 for the fourth time. Two implementations of one rule always end up with two behaviours; the divergence showed as 280 evidenced items against 1,692 by manual computation.
lessons.caughtBy: a backfill number that was far too large a drop to be explained by the change made

guards.contains: the gate agrees with a manual computation

lessons.mistake: form-standard-relevance was measured on the RENDERED student surface, which strips the key by design. An item asking about 'Marshall's speech' names the Marshall Plan only in its correct answer, so it read as naming nothing and a green form went red for a reason that was an artefact of the measurement. Relevance is a property of the ITEM, not of the printed page — the inverse of L34, where a bank gate was wrongly run over a rendered form.
lessons.caughtBy: a regression on a form that had been green through three previous tightenings

guards.contains: Relevance is a property of the ITEM
the form runner passes source items

lessons.mistake: 19 of 94 standards are identifiable by fewer than two signals, and 9 by none. US.25's only signal is 'World War I', so an extended-response essay on American imperialism 1890-1914 matched it and would have printed under 'causes of World War I'. A relevance verdict on such a standard is soft, and that is a disclosed limitation rather than something to hide behind a green gate — the readiness report now carries identifyingSignals and weaklyIdentifiable per standard. [2026-09-03: the '9 identifiable by none' half of this became L51/L52 — the count was recorded here and never acted on, and a limitation nothing enforces is a note, not a guard. US.25 itself is no longer weak; the proof moved to US.65, which still is.]
lessons.caughtBy: reading a selected item and disagreeing with the match that admitted it

lessons.mistake: The choice-length gate was UNSATISFIABLE below four items. With n=2 the only possible shares are 0%, 50% and 100%, none of which falls in the 15-35% band, so a two-item draft could never pass however it was written. A gate that cannot be satisfied is worse than no gate: it blocks work rather than catching a defect, and it is the L05/L33 lesson in the one shape that stops everything.
lessons.caughtBy: the first clean generated draft being refused by a gate it could not satisfy

guards.contains: the tolerance band is unreachable at that size

lessons.mistake: The migrated bank was generated against a REAL specification — IRT parameters on 100% of 5,045 items, DOK levels on 100%, blueprint structure, item-writing conventions — and still shipped the key as the longest choice 53% of the time, 920 explanations restating the key, and DOK rationales on 8.7%. The spec was satisfied in FORM and not in SUBSTANCE, and nothing measured the difference. A parameter present in a field is indistinguishable from a parameter that means something. That is why generation is now gated BEFORE admission rather than reviewed after: tools/submit_items.py refuses a draft that fails any item-level gate, and the draft does not enter the bank at all.
lessons.caughtBy: measuring conformance against substance on a bank that was fully conformant

guards.contains: satisfied in FORM and not in SUBSTANCE

lessons.mistake: relevance_scan SKIPPED, silently and without counting, every item whose standard carried no identifying signal. Nine of the 94 standards have no proper noun in their sentence — US.13 'working conditions ... women and children as a labor source', US.69 'atomic testing / civil defense / mutual assured destruction', US.67 'television and mass media' — so 331 servable items claiming them were judged by nobody. The relevance gate read PASS over a population it never looked at, and the readiness report printed those standards at '0 aligned', which reads as 'no items exist' rather than 'no item here can ever be checked'. This is the whole-gate vacuous-pass defect of L11/L15 one level down, per standard, where the `judged` counter cannot see it because the gate is busy judging 3,600 other items. A gate green against nothing is the most dangerous result there is, and it reads exactly like a clean pass.
lessons.caughtBy: asking why 19 standards showed zero aligned items, and finding that 9 of them had items — just no way to judge them

guards.contains: a standard with NO judgeable signal FAILS the gate
is RETURNED as unjudgeable rather than dropped

lessons.mistake: The relevance matcher required a CAPITALISED NAME. That is right for 'Sherman Antitrust Act' and structurally blind to a third of the state's sentences, which are about common-noun content: working conditions, imperialists and non-imperialists, radio and movies, flappers and birth control, the baby boomer generation, mutual assured destruction. Those standards were not hard to match — they were impossible to match, and nothing in the system said so. topic_signals() reads the whole sentence (not just the 'including' checklist, which three of them do not have) and holds a higher sufficiency bar because a common noun is looser than a name: one multi-word phrase, or two distinct single words. Measured against 400 sampled items it claims FEWER standards per item than the proper-noun matcher already accepted (0.77 vs 1.22), so it is not a loosening — and every stoplist word in it was curated from measurement, not intuition ('civil' alone matched civil war, civil rights and civil defense indiscriminately).
lessons.caughtBy: measuring identifying_signals() across all 94 standards instead of trusting it

guards.contains: ONE single word is NOT evidence
a bare abstraction is never a topic signal

lessons.mistake: backfill_alignment.py wrote alignmentStatus UNCONDITIONALLY on every record, so the next run after a human review pass would have erased every 'human-verified' stamp — a recorded fact about work a person actually did, silently replaced by a recomputation. No item carried that status yet, which is the only reason it had not happened. The same tool also decided which items were 'judged' using standard_signals() — a THIRD definition, looser than the one relevance_scan judges on — so an item could be marked judged here and skipped there. L22's shape again: a rule with two implementations has two behaviours.
lessons.caughtBy: reading backfill_alignment.py while changing what 'judgeable' means

guards.contains: backfill judges on the SAME signals

lessons.mistake: HANDOFF.md opens by saying its numbers were MEASURED, and nothing re-measured them. One change moved aligned items 1,890->2,006, buildable standards 55->66 and the ledger 50/109->53/125, and every one of those figures sat in the handoff still reading as a current fact. Same defect as a reference build named in prose and never re-measured: a number in prose is a CLAIM, and an unmeasured claim rots silently while continuing to look authoritative. Worse, the FIRST version of the check re-derived the readiness total instead of calling the tool, and got 1,763 against the tool's 1,867 — it pooled items by standardCodes and skipped the per-standard relevance rule. A checker written to catch drift, drifting: L22 for the seventh time. form_readiness.rows() is now the one implementation and the checker calls it.
lessons.caughtBy: noticing that the handoff's own numbers were stale in the same commit that changed them

guards.contains: the readiness total comes from the TOOL

lessons.mistake: A form that mixed 12 selected-response items with 6 extended responses/DBQs shipped GREEN on 23 gates and READ as a test form. Sean, on his first teacher pass: 'this is a mixed classroom assessment, not a TCAP-field-testable form.' Nothing in the artifact said which it was, because nothing in the artifact COULD: tcapFormat existed on 0 of 3,958 servable items, a rubric on 0 of 100 constructed-response and document-based items, and a bias/sensitivity review on none at all. Not thin — ABSENT, everywhere, while every structural gate read green. tcapFormat now defaults to false with a stated reason and has NO automatic path to true: a machine affirming its own field-testability is exactly the unverified compliance claim this repo refuses to make.
lessons.caughtBy: Sean reading the rendered form as a teacher, which is the one measurement no gate performs

guards.contains: claiming field-testability with no human affirmation FAILS
a CARRIER does not count as a rubric

lessons.mistake: The teacher key printed 'KEY: B · DOK 1 · US.46' and stopped. Sean: the selected-response items 'lack the required standards, DOK/Hess, distractor, bias, citation, and IRT metadata in the supplied form.' Every one of those fields was IN THE RECORD and none of it reached the PAGE — and a field present in a record and absent from the page is, to the person holding the page, not present. The gates measured the student surface for leakage and never asked whether the teacher surface carried what a teacher needs to judge an item's rigour, fairness or fit. gate_form_teacher_metadata now reads the rendered teacher PDF and counts each required row against the number of keyed items, so an analysis block that renders once and silently stops fails rather than passing on one sighting.
lessons.caughtBy: Sean naming the six missing metadata families after reading the printed key

lessons.mistake: THE WORST ONE IN THIS PASS. The form builder re-letters choices to de-bias key position — that is what key_targets() is for — and 2,440 of 3,928 servable items hard-code a choice letter inside their explanation. So FORM-A item 1 keyed C in the bank, rendered as 'KEY: B', and printed 'B is incorrect because it describes a different program' directly underneath. Five items on FORM-A and one on FORM-B did this, on a form both this system and its twenty-two gates called GREEN. Every gate that could have caught it was measuring the RECORD, where the letters were perfectly self-consistent; the contradiction only exists on the rendered page. remap_letters() rewrites letter references through the builder's own permutation (a remap, not authoring, and deliberately NOT idempotent), and gate_form_key_contradiction reads the rendered teacher PDF rather than trusting that the remap was written correctly. Proved by disabling the remap and watching the gate go red on all five.
lessons.caughtBy: reading one rendered teacher key line by line after Sean's note, instead of reading the records

guards.contains: an explanation that calls the KEY wrong FAILS

lessons.mistake: 79 of the bank's 100 extended-response items ALREADY had a complete scoring guide — band by band, 0 through 6 — sitting inside the `explanation` field, which the teacher key prints under the heading 'Why the key is right'. A six-band rubric rendered as the answer rationale for a document-based question is not something a teacher can score from, and no gate could see it because `explanation` was populated and every check on it was a presence check. L50's shape exactly: satisfied in form, not in substance. extract_rubrics.py moves them into a structured field verbatim and REPORTS the ones that do not parse rather than guessing — a rubric invented to fill a field is the carrier defect wearing a better disguise.
lessons.caughtBy: reading the four constructed responses the rubric gate failed, and finding three of the DBQs already carried what it was asking for

lessons.mistake: apply_rubrics.py refused all four correctly-written rubrics because it required every band descriptor to be 40+ characters, and the ZERO band's descriptor is legitimately 'No response, or off-topic.' An alarm that fires on the harmless is how someone learns to pass --force, and this repo has now made that mistake twice (L49: the choice-length gate was unsatisfiable below four items). A validation floor must be checked against a CORRECT input before it is trusted, not only against a defective one.
lessons.caughtBy: the tool refusing my own drafts

guards.contains: The ZERO band is legitimately short
validate accepts a short ZERO band

lessons.mistake: The assessment builder's blueprint REQUIRED a constructed response and a document-based question to reach its highest tier, so the builder was structurally obliged to produce the mixed instructional packet Sean objected to: 'this is a mixed classroom assessment, not a TCAP-field-testable form ... all the questions on the assessment builder need to be TCAP-style multiple choice, maybe multiple select.' The four-tier ladder had been built to answer a real problem — DOK-4 is impossible in a four-option item — but it answered it by putting an extended item on a test form rather than by saying on the page that a selected-response form cannot reach DOK-4. The blueprint now declares surface: assessment and allowedItemTypes, the tiers are selected-response only with a printed DOK ceiling of 3, and gate_form_surface holds the artifact to it. Buildable standards went 66 -> 73 as a side effect: the DBQ requirement was what most standards could not meet.
lessons.caughtBy: Sean, reading the form as a teacher and naming what it was

lessons.mistake: The DBQ parser knew ONE of the two stem formats in this bank and reported '0 doc(s)' for the other — which reads as 'this item has no sources' rather than 'this parser cannot see them', the same confusion as a standard with no signals reading as 'no items exist' (L51). 26 of 34 DBQs used the second shape (DOCUMENT 1 / Source: / excerpt, separated by box-drawing rules) rather than the first. Four more parsed their documents and reported no PROMPT, because a stem with no closing separator leaves the prompt inside the last document's body. Coverage was MEASURED across all 34 before the builder was trusted, not sampled on the one item I happened to be reading.
lessons.caughtBy: running --list across all 34 items instead of building the one I had open

guards.contains: TWO stem formats live in this bank

lessons.mistake: THE THIRD OVER-EAGER MATCHER (after L49 and L59), and this time two in one gate pass. activity-teacher-isolation matched the substring 'scoring guide' and failed all 34 student sheets on their own footer — 'its scoring guide is not calibrated' — which is the sheet honestly disclosing itself. activity-sourcing took the first quotation mark as the citation/excerpt boundary and so measured a citation that quotes a title (George Kennan, “The Long Telegram,”) as 15 characters, failing three correctly-sourced cards; it also counted the planning table's 'Document C' row as a source card, inflating the population from 172 to 348. In all three cases the boundary was chosen from what USUALLY appears rather than from what the builder actually emits — the excerpt's opening quote is inserted by CSS ::before as U+201C, which is a construction guarantee, and a heading is anchored to its line. A gate must be run against KNOWN-CLEAN output before it is trusted, not only against a defect.
lessons.caughtBy: my own new gates failing my own new deliverable, and checking the artifact rather than believing them

lessons.mistake: The review queue became one person's bottleneck — two sessions put 10 items, 83 rubrics, 30 held records and 7 citations on the only reviewer this project has — and the obvious fix is the one that would have destroyed the bank. An AI pass that writes approvals empties the queue and removes the reason a district could trust any of it, INVISIBLY, because an approval record looks identical whoever wrote it: every gate would still read green and nothing on the page would say a machine had signed off on machine work. So the first pass triages and drafts and never approves. It writes only into an `aiReview` namespace that counts toward no gate, satisfies no provenance and lets nothing ship; every verdict carries its EVIDENCE and its CANNOT-VERIFY list, because a verdict with no evidence is an opinion and a reviewer that never says 'I don't know' is not reviewing; and `clear-recommended` is permitted only on the four deterministic classes the policy declares, so anything touching history, a citation, Spanish, bias or a rubric descriptor escalates even when it looks easy. Enforced on the RECORDS, not on the reviewer's source, because a tool can be rewritten and a policy file is prose until something reads it. Proved on all eight ways across the line. The gate then failed a FORM for judging nothing — no item on it carried an AI review — which is the alarm-on-the-harmless pattern a fourth time (L49, L59, L62). 'Nothing here claims review' is true and safe; 'this was not measured' is a different statement. It is N/A with a stated reason now, and the population is any review claim of either kind.
lessons.caughtBy: asking what the queue fix would cost before building it

lessons.mistake: I created 79 items of review debt out of nothing. Extracting the scoring guides out of the `explanation` field and into a structured `rubric` field stamped every one `needs-review` — but none of that content was new. All 79 were migrated or provisional bank text moving fields UNCHANGED, zero carried authored provenance, and the extraction gate already proved the move was faithful. They were never Sean's to review, and they inflated his queue from 40 to 119. Review debt is the scarcest resource in this project: he is the only reviewer it has, so a queue padded with work nobody needed to do is not a neutral error — it buries the ten rows that genuinely need a person and it teaches whoever is reading to skim. A structural relocation does not create a review obligation; relocated content inherits the item's status and says so. `needs-review` on a component is now a claim that something was AUTHORED, and gate_review_debt fails anything else. Related: asking a reviewer to compose 30 replacement sentences when 28 of them only need one sentence deleted is the same waste in a different shape — the pass now checks whether a finished argument survives the deletion and drafts the before/after.
lessons.caughtBy: Sean asking a question that made me re-examine what was actually on his desk

guards.contains: A structural relocation does not create a review
a RELOCATED rubric may not be flagged needs-review

lessons.mistake: EVERY new gate I add reports NOT MEASURED the first time it is scoped to a form, and NOT MEASURED fails all-gates-measured. It has now happened five times — the choice-length cue below four items (L49), the rubric-descriptor floor on a correct zero band (L59), two matchers on the DBQ activities (L62), ai-review-boundary on a form nobody had AI-reviewed, and review-debt on a selected-response form that carries no rubrics. The vacuous-pass discipline is right and is not what is failing: 'nothing here has a rubric' and 'this was not measured' are different statements, and only the first is true. A gate whose population can legitimately be empty in a narrower scope needs an N/A path WITH A STATED REASON, written at the same time as the gate — not after the pipeline fails. The tell is the same every time: I write the gate against the bank, where its population is never empty, and never run it against a form before wiring it.
lessons.caughtBy: the pipeline, five times, which is four times more than it should have taken

lessons.mistake: scaffold_course.py --all --apply overwrote blueprints/us-history-geography.blueprint.json, which was not a placeholder — it was carrying the form ladder (three tiers), the DOK-ceiling disclosure text and the bank measurement target that the form builder and five gates read. The new blueprint was correct about everything it knew and silent about everything it did not, so the damage surfaced one KeyError at a time: form['tiers'], then bp['defaults'], then bank['proportionTolerance']. Nothing said 'you are about to replace a live file'. A scaffolder is for standing a course UP; pointed at one already carrying work it is a deletion tool with a helpful name. Two guards: the tool now REFUSES to overwrite an existing binding or blueprint without --force and names what would be lost, and the course-independent form ladder is carried INTO every scaffold so a new course cannot be born without the tiers its gates resolve against. Related: the bank measurement target is now the blueprint's OWN computed DOK distribution rather than an inherited hard-coded 33/33/17/17 that reserved 17% for DOK-4 — a level a selected-response bank can never contain.
lessons.caughtBy: running the form gates immediately after the scaffold, on the suspicion that --all --apply had touched more than it should

lessons.mistake: The misconception taxonomy nearly got built bottom-up. The plan was to mine it from the 11,379 distractors already in the bank, on the reasoning that a distractor written to be wrong implies the misconception it targets. Measured first: only 66 of 11,379 carry any explanation of WHY they are wrong, and all 66 are ones authored in this session. There was nothing to mine. Inferring 11,313 misconceptions from bare distractor TEXT would have been AI reading intent into content whose author never stated one, at scale, into the field the entire analytics layer depends on. The taxonomy is built top-down from the standards instead, and the structural families are a design artifact marked DRAFT pending a human read.
lessons.caughtBy: measuring the source before building the tool that would have consumed it

guards.contains: A family ID recurs across items

lessons.mistake: Every gate in this repo judged ONE form, and 'five parallel tests, equal in rigor, testing the same content' is a claim about a SET. Five forms could each pass all 31 gates and still be five different tests — differing item count, DOK profile, or which standards they touched — because the divergence is invisible one form at a time. gate_form_parallelism compares every member against the first on count, standards, DOK distribution, item types and stimulus mix, and fails ANY shared item: a student retaking Form C after Form A must not meet the same question twice or the retake measures memory. gate_family_coverage fails a family that CLAIMS full-course coverage without having it, while a partial family passes and states its share — a unit test is not the whole course and must not be failed for it. Proved by mutating a RENDERED member on disk, not a stub, because the gates read manifests and student surfaces and a hand-built dict would prove only that they can read one.
lessons.caughtBy: asking what measures 'parallel' before generating 4,380 items against the word

lessons.mistake: forms/families/ holds family manifests, not a form, and BOTH the gate runner and the status report treated it as a rendered form because each globbed forms/* for itself. The runner emitted six phantom 'families/...' gate results; the status report crashed on a missing manifest.json. One rule with two implementations, which is this repo's most repeated defect — itemio.form_dirs() is now the single definition and both call it. Separately: a family MEMBER has no tier, because its shape comes from the family allocation rather than the tier ladder, so form-blueprint returns N/A with that reason instead of failing a correctly-built form for not being something it never claimed to be.
lessons.caughtBy: check-reports-fresh, which caught the status report crashing on the same bad assumption
